top_comments.author: @ke6gwf
top_comments.text:
*sigh... News people and heavy equipment names.... Lol

So, cranes lift loads suspended by cables. 
Personal lifts lift people in baskets.

The one lifting the workers in this video is a boom lift, looks like a JLG judging by the color. One I have seen in other of Mary's pictures has a 125 foot reach, but most are up to 60 foot. 
Very likely this one. 
https://www.jlg.com/equipment/engine-powered-boom-lifts/articulating/1250ajp-articulating-boom-lift

The ones that just lift straight up that they have there are scissor lifts, and they usually go up to 20 to 30 feet.

If you just want the generic term, manlift or personal lift works, but the ones with a long hydraulic boom, are called boom lifts.

top_comments.author: @thomaseo1
top_comments.text:
They really should invest in some friction stir welding especially for the tank. From what I understand fsw retains at least 80% or higher of the strength of the material whereas stick welding gives it something like 45 to 50%. They currently use fsw for Falcon, SLS and Vulcan. Fsw will also allow you to weld dissimilar sizes and even materials if necessary, it also work good with stainless steel. 
It's major drawbacks are that you have to have large clamps holding down the sheetS, is highly specialized, chews through bits fairly quickly and is pretty expensive.

So my bet is that until they start doing FSW on critical Parts like the tank, I think Starship will weigh more than it should and will continue having problems with critical welds on the tank sections.

top_comments.text: NOTE: Crane audio was transmitted via a public frequency and was captured using the same methods used to listen to pilots and air traffic control.

top_comments.author: @ke6gwf
top_comments.text:
"Boom down, hold the load" is moving the load away from the crane while maintaining the height.
It requires using the winch to Cable Up at the same time, and same speed, as the load is lowering with the boom tilting down.
It basically transits the load horizontally away from the crane.

They are running under positive control here, where if they stop talking, the crane operator will stop moving.
If they were in visual range, it would be hand signals, which are continous.

Since the crane op doesn't know if the load is supposed to keep moving, or the spotter forgot to key his microphone or had his battery die, the spotter has to keep singing.

The crane winch drum has markings on the rim that the operator can see, so he knows exactly how much cable he's letting out.
They generally also have a clicker that makes a sound every 6 inches or something so the operator can tell by ear how fast the cable is moving.
And on a fancy crane like that, I am sure it has a readout showing how many inches the cable has moved.

They also have a load cell, often built into the hook assembly, to show them the weight they are picking up.
That's how he knows how heavy it is. And the "deduct" they asked a

(yes,  primary mission did go well - but mid accent engine shutdown isn't ideal) Elon saying "This vehicle has seen a lot of wear, so today isn’t a big surprise." on Twitter, could indicate that this engine shutdown could somehow be related to reuse.

Five flights compared to Discovery's 39 flights - ain't much but thats 5x times more any other orbiter class booster today has flown. Goes to show you how successful SpaceX's reuse program is thus far. Hope to see Blue and Rocket Lab see similar success!
Sorry I was thinking about this and had to share it with somebody. Also sorry if this cmt was posted multiple times - I hit "post" once and for some reason it got posted 4 times (why?)

One area that still is a big question mark with offshore launch facility is the effect of sound waves on marine envrironment. There is also the portential for acoustical amplification with support legs, tethers, empty fuel tanks etc. I will be very interested to see SpaceX solutions to this potential issue long term. Also the floating LNG production platforms used in Australia, which are closest conceptually to what Spacex will utilise, have extreme fire & safety protocols in place which are not general population friendly. So a combined refueling\passenger embarking platform with processing facilities in close proximity is going to be a massive challenge.
! would think baby steps would be to look at remote land\island based infrastructure for initial network that can then be repurposed as emergency backup in the event of in-flight problems, which then gives time to develop & get approval for floating platforms.

top_comments.author: @ArcadiyIvanov
top_comments.text:
34:00 Physics does work out that way. When cryogenic liquid is boiling, the boiling part may be cold relative to the ambient but it's still the most energetic part of the cryogenic liquid. So as the most energetic cold molecules escape the total liquid temperature is dropping. Boiling is just a very energetic evaporation, and evaporation at room temperature or at cryogenic temperature always lowers the temperature of what remains as the molecules that do NOT evaporate actually end up to be the coldest ones. 
That's why the cold gas thrusters on Falcon 9 first stage in vacuum  show up as non-transparent (i.e. white plumes): as soon as the gas is released the most energetic molecules escape rapidly and the remaining immediately crystallize into solid ice skipping the liquid stage as the low energy of molecules that do not immediately escape allows them to form a solid as they simply don't fly away from each other fast enough.

Working in high tech labs to the tune of $18.6 billion to date, Boeing has spent a decade trying to get the SLS flying. When flying, if ever, each launch will cost a minimum of $2 billion with nonreusable hardware. 
Here, Musk's "rocket cowboys" working in open fields in the rain, have done more in the last year to change the face of powered space flight than at any other time in history. Starship projected launch cost: $2 million per flight, each ship, and booster fully reusable. Watching these cowboys work fills me with a sense of pride. 
The big question, why does SLS even exist in the same universe as SpaceX?

top_comments.author: @rajusapkota5623
top_comments.text: I am working at construction of Power Plant as lead material Inspector. We use 304L/304 steel excessively in the high pressure and extreme heat area. It is very durable under high pressure and high heat area. Here we mostly use low carbon variant of 304 i.e. 304L (even though 304 is structurally slightly stronger than 304L) because 304L alloy’s has lower carbon content which helps to minimize/eliminate carbide precipitation during the welding process and it degrade much slower. Carbon content in 304 is 0.08 and 304L is 0.03. The higher carbon content make 304 slightly stronger but the same thing make it degrade much faster at weld joint in severe corrosive environment. So I think they are using low carbon variant in Starship even though they have to give-up little bit of strength and using 304L eliminates the need to anneal weld joints prior to using the completed metal form—saving time, effort and whole process which delay the project and it became costly coz they need to do it in each and every weld no matter the size. Its Spacex and "The best process is no process"- Elon Musk.

top_comments.author: @Naultarous
top_comments.text:
57:30 Very important note.  SN's are not Starships.  They are parts of Starships. Yes large parts but you have to take that into account. SLS is a full 100% system. How much of the Starship would you say is complete so far? Tanks and engines at 90%, cargo and nose sections to 5%, landing aero surfaces to 50%, primary booster (SH) to 5 or 10%. 
If you want to compare apples to apples as full system to launch, to be fair, it's a lot closer than number of vehicles. I think SpaceX will win the race but discounting SLS is a mistake.

Thank you to Chris B for bringing it back to more logical thinking.  This is why you are awesome.

top_comments.author: @rev.markcarrier1894
top_comments.text: The pace of Starship development, construction, and testing reminds me very much of the 1960’s.  We went from Project Mercury in the early part of the decade to Project Gemini almost immediately afterwards, and then Apollo in 1967.  And they were building prototypes of the Saturn V all the while.  Also during this time were the first probes to the Moon, Venus, and Mars.  It seemed like something new and fantastic happened every day.  At night, after a TV show was over, there would be special reports, not very long, featuring the latest pictures of Mars from Mariners 6 and 7.  My parents would hustle me out of bed to see them.  It was an exciting time to be alive. There is much dissension in our country now just as then, but these are even more exciting times.  A hundred years from now no one will remember who was president or what the social situation was like in the U.S. But everyone will know this was the time when the human race began to move into the solar system.

top_comments.author: @GenoLoma
top_comments.text:
With all these walls and shipping containers being put along the fanceline, soon we're gonna need to get Mary a bus for them to fit out with roof mounted cameras.. seems the only way.. ;)
I guess SpaceX is thinking of Security, and possibly windbreaks for the ground staff, but as far as us, the viewing pubic, goes, there's no chance of us gaining any I.P. secrets by watching the assembly of these amazing vehicles out in the open..
And besides, anything which IS I.P. sensitive can be done in the tents they already have..
Also, if SpaceX bring Mary onside, they can instruct on what can, and in certain circumstances can not, be filmed, if that's an issue..
SpaceX has a huge, almost cult, following now, mainly due to the tireless work of Mary and the NSF team.. why would they want to cripple that with some old shipping containers?
It'd be truly awesome for Mary to have onsite, authorised access to document the build process of these vehicles, and I think that would only serve to massively increase the popularity of what they are doing there in Boca..

top_comments.text: It still amazes me to watch SpaceX install this extremely sophisticated hardware using rental equipment, outdoors, on a crude concrete pad next to a dirt berm. For forty years I was convinced that this could only happen in massive assembling buildings with purpose built lifts, glossy white floors and in time frames of weeks or months with technicians checking every bolt electronically for micro-defects. The industrial path from what SpaceX is doing now to fully fledged mass production has never been clearer. Sometimes to move forward you need to take a step back.

top_comments.author: @maxsemple7898
top_comments.text: Something I think isn't really pointed out enough when talking test regimes is that most rocket companies are developing fairly traditional styles of rocket. These types saw plenty of explosions when first being developed back in the 50s and 60s. Starship is a brand new concept when it comes to the landing style - the first flight proving and model validation was SN8, and to be fair it came pretty close to landing. If you are comparing the amount of blown up vehicles I think you need to compare back to the original rockets when NASA were developing for the mercury programme, not just comparing the amount blown up of starship Vs SLS

top_comments.text: While Mary rightly gets the attention for her great picture & video, I'd like to give a BIG shout out to Derek, who puts it all together for these marvelous videos. I'm 74 years old and my career was television, so I know a little about what you're doing, Derek. These videos are absolutely priceless. When I watch, I'm taken by the way you speed up some scenes in such a way as to closely resemble historical black and white newsreels from my generation. The effect is surreal for me, and I think it's a part of why so many comment about the historical nature of what you're doing. You're presenting these pictures as historical videos, and I suspect you are uniquely aware of what that means. Thank you. And mostly, well done!

GalagaChamp  - I get my data on orbits from Space-Track.org and from

? : How's our next X-ray telescope looking: Well, we're all on
tenterhooks waiting for the "Decadal Survey" to report its
recommendations. Stay tuned this summer.

Space Junkie:  The amount of space debris: about 20000 tracked objects
of which 16000 are junk and 4000 are active satellites. Plus many more  
tiny pieces of debris that are too small to track.  The most common kind
of space debris is shrapnel from exploded rocket stages which had

top_comments.author: @markamy357
top_comments.text:
Guys I’m sensing a lot of negativity about the tiles but when the tank is filled with Ln2 it shrinks considerably which can be partly offset by the degree of pressurization, this can cause the edges of the tiles to squeeze together and break. In the test Spacex may have been seeing how far they can push this, they may have for instance had the tiles close together , the pressure low, and the tank extremely cold
As for the top group of tiles there is a large butterfly vent very close to these tiles, I have seen a close up of it and the butterfly disc in the valve is positioned such that at partial opened position the blast of pressure doesn’t shoot straight out but will be directed straight towards the edge of those tiles and blasting under through the ceramic fiber blanket, and creating excess pressures underneath effortlessly popping them off.

top_comments.author: @terpcj
top_comments.text:
I remember back during the Apollo XII moonwalk, upon seeing how all the science equipment was covered in dust and regolith, Pete Conrad chuckled about how, during training, the scientists and engineers were so concerned that their clean experiments be kept clean. 

There are two ways you can build rockets: 1) in aerospace cathedrals kept as tidy and dust-free as possible; or 2) out in the open, facing nature, just like they'll have to be when actually being used. You have a choice about whether to build a fussy sports car that needs to be tended to by fancy equipment and whose body is buffed up with lambswool, or you can have a muscle car whose engine you can tear down and rebuild in your garage and body work is handled with a hammer, a torch, and some Bondo.

We rag on the "primitive" soviet-era rocket machines, but they've managed to keep flying for over fifty years. It's like Scotty warned us: "The more they overthink the plumbing, the easier it is to stop up the drain."

top_comments.text:
I learned in Hawaii that, while there are neither hurricane nor earthquake "proof" structures, you can in fact build "highly resistant" ones. Given the meat on those H beams (2"?), the very dense bolting pattern, and robust triangulation and gusseting of the new structural members  the designers have taken the threat more seriously at the Thicc Bay than on the previous large enclosed structures for whatever reason.

 This may simply be due to the greater cross section of the new Thicc Bay, or a greater appreciation for potential high wind hazards of the location in general, something my personal experience has lead me to consider all along. If they begin strengthening the high and mid bays too then the latter case is more likely. Oy, and the 'tents'/ tensioned membrane structures are much stronger than they look, but flying debris could be very bad, with the tearing. What do Civil Engineers do? Worry.

top_comments.author: @MichaelSmith-iw5cs
top_comments.text:
The delivery @ 6:27 is what we call a "canned" vertical turbine pump, and appears to be 4 or 5 stages (kinda hard to tell closer to the discharge head) if you look at the shot at 6:44. The pump is installed into a "can" that is installed into the ground, fluid enters the inlet flange (it's sitting on it on the left side), and enters the pump via the suction bell (on the right end of the pump), and is pumped up through 4 or 5 impellers until coming out the exit flange (pointing straight up).

My guess is a cryo pump. Usually you use this style for applications where your NPSHA/NPSHR ratio (basically your inlet pressure available vs required) is close to 1. I would think we'd see a horizontal style pump for the water deluge system, but it wouldn't be out of the question for this to be used for water. I can't really say for certain, but I'd guess impeller diameters are probably in the 24" range.

top_comments.author: @johnwerner8108
top_comments.text: I think there's a lot more going on here than SpaceX just filling up the tanks and looking for leaks. If it were me I would chill the engines (concurrent or consecutively) and check how all the temperature sensors (RTDs, thermocouples, etc.) are reading back to the system and ultimately, the control room. This has to be a tremendous amount of I/O (input/output devices) to monitor, trend and calibrate. Not just on the engines but throughout the ship. And not just temp. but pressure, level, flow. The discrete and analog devices involved with Starship have always been an area of great interest to me but nobody ever goes into those type details.

some viewing notes:
- A "lightbulb bulb went on" and SpaceX ha snow deployed moveable scaffolding systems called "skyclimber" brand units, instead of adding and removing small sections of scaffolding when doing work on the tower column tracks.
- The closeup views of the tower QD arm these days, with workers "inside" help to understand how gigantic the tower QD arm is, twice the height of the workers inside, and big enough that they can walk around inside the tower QD arm as though it is a "room". 
- Not only is the dirt berm gone, but it looks like SpaceX could be just days away from working on creating the concrete foundations and moat walls and such, to be able to add 2 more horizontal lch4 tanks next to the existing pair. 
- SpaceX is running liquid gas lines, underground, from the orbital tank farm over to the suborbital pads, apparently to be able to perform cryo tests and such at the suborbital pads, but using the orbital tank farm's gases. 
- It looks like there are 2 doors now and a balcony so that people can walk back and forth between the 2 halves of the "sky bar" on top of the high bay (just had to keep evolving it).
- OMG! Starbase is just endlessly exciting!

top_comments.author: @GoCoyote
top_comments.text: What you call "venting" can also be 'purging or flushing,' and 'pressure or functional testing,' using liquid or gaseous nitrogen, or other inert gas. When pipes designed to carry specific gases like methane or LOX are constructed, they will have soiling, moisture, welding materials, and atmospheric air inside of them. They will need to be flushed and purged of all gas and materials that may effect valve function, cause corrosion to the pipes, cause contamination, or react negatively to the material being transported in the piping. LOX will react, often violently, to anything that oxidizes that is in the piping. The nitrogen will remove moisture and materials from the piping, and can be left pressurized to ensure the pipe remains leak free until used for its intended purpose.

Now, c'mon FAA, everyone is waiting on you, stop dragging your feet and lets get with it!

top_comments.text: While it can be argued that right now, March 2022, there is nothing competitive with the SLS, in that there is nothing else powerful enough to deliver an Orion capsule to Lunar orbit, that will not be true in May 2024, 26 months from now when the first operational flight is scheduled.    By the end of 2022, Starship will be capable of carrying the entire Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage (ICPS) plus its payload to the planned initial 0 x 1,791km elliptical orbit.  The ICPS masses 31,000kg is 13m tall and 5m and the Orion CM with the ESM is 26,000 kg and 7.3m tall.  That is a total payload of 47 tonnes and height of 20.3 m, which is technically just over the current announced height of the Starship payload bay, but SpaceX is already considering stretching Starship, and the ICPS and Orion do not require an external fairing.  The Orion Launch Abort System is not necessary because the Starship itself should be capable of escaping a booster failure, especially in the version with 9 engines. For everyone out there that think this whole process (ie, testing and launching of the 1st starship) is taking too long, just look at the timeliness from other space organisations! re: moon landers.
A Semi truck and a Jeep both are useful, and neither is really a replacement for the other. Dynetics is a Jeep, Starship is a Semi, both should be available. Use the Dynetics for exploration and the Starship for delivering infrastructure and supplies. 

The fact that a Starship can be delivered for anything approaching a similar cost to Dynetics points out how far ahead SpaceX is and how much trouble everyone else is going to be in over the next decade or so (probably longer, counting how fast other companies develop their rockets.

I would love to see a proposal from SpaceX that sent a starship to the moon, and took along a Dynetics as payload for local hops.

videos.title: Is the FAA to blame for Starship delays?

top_comments.author: @xlUIblisUlx
top_comments.text:
I think you're largely ignoring the explanatory power of Parkinson's Law here: The work will expand to fill the time allotted. If you reverse the causality, the various regulatory delays that have prevented SpaceX from conducting validation testing involving launches from Boca Chica can themselves be the explanation for SpaceX's alternative focus on redesigning Raptor, building out a sophisticated GSE operation, reimagining a more mass-efficient landing procedure with a catch-tower, etc. These tasks obviously delay the launch of "Starship 2" - a system that now requires a sophisticated Stage 0 platform to start the booster engines, and a catch tower to catch the vehicles - but would not necessarily have delayed "Starship 1", an MVP with landing legs, and more complex engines that would have been more difficult to manufacture.

If we imagine an alternate universe, with no regulatory delays, SpaceX may instead have been more interested in launching an "orbital MVP" to test aspects of re-entry/tiles, refueling, etc. during this period, and maybe they would have done this whole "redesign of Raptor" and "overbuild the GSE" at a later date, to improve the economic viability of the progra

top_comments.author: @ranchis9044
top_comments.text: Highly speculative, I personaly want to believe if FAA had let the original Enviromental statement stand, SpaceX would have gone ahead with launches even with suboptimal conditions, They never showed the slightest fear of failure with past launches so there is no reason to believe they would willingly "choose" to wait until every detail of stage 0 was perfect, and wait for raptor 2 development. These developments would have eventually happened but launch attempts equal hard data and without the data, booster 7 and ship 24 are still just their best guess instead of an iteration based on solid data

top_comments.author: @wulf2121
top_comments.text: I have some speculation what this chopstick testing might have been good for: Obviously the chopsticks never would need to be in that last position relative to the orbital launch table during stacking or landing operations. But if you look  at the position of the arms relative to the booster and imagine both the arms and the booster being in the air, this would be how the arms see the booster coming in during the landing (after engines already are below the arms). So the purpose of this could be collecting sensor data and camera images to train the system that detects the exact position of the booster during landing in order to move the arms to the correct position.

top_comments.author: @knowledgeisgood9645
top_comments.text:
Some ask why the chopsticks were not used instead of the crane. I think there are at least 3 reasons.
To begin with we don't know if the hydraulics are fixed or not (I think they are but I don't know).
They are installing pistons and shock absorbers to lift and lower the rails that hold the booster or ship (to dampen the jolt of landing). They are also installing what looks like rubber pads on the sides, to avoid metal on metal bumps. (BTW, have you noticed the "ramp" extension of the stringers around the lifting hooks on the booster? I think those are to smoothly glide on when landing.)
Until all that work is done it would not be advisable to use the chopsticks.

top_comments.author: @NASASpaceflight
top_comments.text:
Apologies for no labels on the clips. That's an error! Won't happen again. Timestamps are in the vid and listed below: Also, daily vids never went away; they just aren't every single day when there wasn't a lot happening. We have SBL 24/7 to cover 12 hours of mount work, as opposed to a daily that's not very interesting. There will be far more dailies when the action picks up, which is coming as Booster 7 returns.

Usual week of Starbase: Starbase Live 24/7. Dailies when there's a "here's a good round up of interesting things". Dedicated commentary livestreams for events like Static Fire tests. Fast turnaround vids of such events. Feature videos (like the Methalox one). And yes, there's been a lot of NSF Livestreams of launches lately recently. Also note, Mary is still with us, but away for personal reasons

top_comments.author: @cogoid
top_comments.text:
20:07 Zylon is yellow Kevlar-like material, produced in Japan by Toyobo Co. Zylon gives strength to the "donuts" and the straps holding the structure together -- as mentioned in the interview. (The orange color comes from the silicone sealant used to make the donuts air-tight.) This part is designed and manufactured by Airborne Systems -- famous for making the best parachutes, including the parachutes used on Mars, in US crewed missions, etc.

The black shiny surface is the heat shielding blanket draped over the donuts. It is a separate component, made by a different company, from very different materials. The outermost layer is made of Hi-Nicalon, a silicon-carbide based cloth, also made in Japan, by Nippon Carbon Co. It is not a new material -- it has been on the market for about 20 years.

How to sew everything together, such that it would withstand the heat of reentry is a very challenging problem, and this is where one of the critical breakthroughs of this project is. Otherwise, the materials themselves are simply purchased from various suppliers.

top_comments.author: @sabyegrp
top_comments.text: I was part of the recovery crew for Apollo 11 and 12 in 1969, the first and second moon landings. Yup, 53 years ago. Each time after the module was brought onboard the USS Hornet and brought down to Hangarbay 2, we were able to get a close up inspection. The foil and bottom heat shield looked just like you see in this video. Burnt to a crisp with most of the foil missing. I have a bunch of slides, (remember those) that I took from the bridge of both recoveries, the landing of the helicopter with the astronauts on the flightdeck, and the eventual lift up of the modules and in Hangarbay 2. It was quite the event in those days. Wish I knew how to attach photos. They are really interesting. Even have a few of President Nixon when he came up on the bridge to watch the recovery.

top_comments.text:
It was cool to watch from 40 miles south in Palm Bay- it pretty much flew overhead, maybe ten degrees from the zenith, and the staging happened just as it got here. I staggered a bit standing in my front yard looking up through binoculars. The plume interactions were gorgeous and I could follow the 2nd stage for a long time to the south but turned to look north for the F9 entry burn. The next part of the light show continued while the rumble from the launch was finally reaching me with a few thumps that sounded from high in the sky from the ascent. The entry booms (four of them, I never heard *that* before) arrived a few minutes later, well after the landing that I didn't see because trees to my north blocked the view.

I think I'll go up to Port Canaveral to watch the Heavy launch Friday, and maybe stop by your operation to say hi.

top_comments.author: @kellyrobinson1780
top_comments.text:
Learning about space, and our place in it, leads to greater understanding of our own planet; and that's not to mention the dozens of satellites in Earth orbit looking back down at us, studying weather, pollution, ocean currents, animal migrations, volcanism, and so much more. We're learning things about Earth that can only be seen from space. And we've created new medicines, and learned more about the human body from experiments in microgravity tha would be impossible on the surface.

Living on the surface, we can only see and learn little bits at a time, like looking at a painting with your nose almost touching it. It's not until you step back and get a little distance that you can see the whole picture.

And the narrator of this short video is right; small, powerful computers, smartphones, "smart" technology, medical scanners, improved communications, better ocean studies, cleaner transportation, cleaner water, recycling techniques, improved batteries, solar energy technology, ALL trace their roots back to our efforts to reach out into space. Our understanding of global warming comes partly from our space programs.

We may soon begin to import minerals and fresh water from astero

top_comments.author: @dphuntsman

top_comments.author: @wdavidwoods
top_comments.text:
On Apollo 12, with the lightning strike and the 'SCE to Aux' call, flight controllers were fully aware that the Saturn V was on target and flying true. The loss of telemetry from the spacecraft was unconnected to the launch vehicle's guidance which was being handled by the Instrument Unit at the top of the Saturn's third stage. The launch vehicle worked perfectly. Flight controllers couldn't see into the spacecraft's systems due to the electrical glitch but at this point, the spacecraft was merely payload. As a student of the Apollo program, I wanted to counter another myth building up around the program.
More on this on the Apollo 12 Flight Journal.
I was surprised that the Apollo 6 flight wasn't mentioned. That really was a close one with major issues in all three stages of the Saturn V.
S-IC first stage - high levels of longitudinal vibration (pogo effect).
S-II second stage - hydrogen leak caused engine shutdown. Crossed wiring also shut down healthy engine.
S-IVB third stage - hydrogen leak caused start tank to not refill. Engine unable to restart.

top_comments.author: @dr4d1s
top_comments.text:
Absolutely fantastic episode but clickbaity title for sure. I literally thought something was wrong with the ISS, our astronauts and/or the next Dragon launch. Please don't do that kinda stuff. You are an accredited space news outlet and not What About It or channels of similar ilk. I have supported you for the past year, and not channels like them, because of your honesty and accuracy. That's why I keep coming back.

I also would have watched the stream if you would have put 50th anniversary of Skylab for the title.

top_comments.author: @starratsstone
top_comments.text: What an absolutely engaging show! I watched it live and am re-watching it now as it was so neat. We need more shows with these stories so that they don't get lost in the grave. Tks NSF!

top_comments.author: @Owencr905
top_comments.text:
Please can we stop these over-exaggerated thumbnails and titles.

I understand that the YouTube algorithm is a mess and you need this stuff to keep new people watching. And I have the upmost respect for the people at NSF.

But this is just not needed, it’s clearly just to grab an extra few views and It ruins the experience for most people.

And it’s not just this, it’s all of your more recent videos. 

Not to mention the constant plugs to your store, the site, other socials, commenting to keep impressions up, sponsors…

It’s just tiring for us loyal fans, I’ve seen the decline over the last few months. The fame is going to someone’s head.

top_comments.author: @Ellhulto
top_comments.text:
B1058 is my favorite booster and B1061 is a close second. 

Why? 
For B1058: Record braking booster launching the first crewed Falcon 9 mission and also NASA logo(s). 
For B1061:
Falcon 9 B1061 first launched Crew-1 to the ISS in November 2020, the first operational flight of Crew Dragon, and landed on a drone ship. It became the first booster to fly crew twice as well as the first reused booster to fly crew as a part of the Crew-2 mission. This first stage went on to complete additional missions. B1061 is the only booster to land on all of SpaceX's different landing zones and drone ships, except LZ-2.

top_comments.author: @Muonium1
top_comments.text: Hubble's gyros have been an issue practically since day 1. Designed in the 70s, they use ultrafine silver-copper alloy wire roughly the diameter of a hair. Immersed in a viscous oil, the original gyros failed quickly due to suspected oxygen dissolved in the oil from pressurization with air for flight. With the problem identified, replacement gyros sent up on subsequent flights were pressurized with pure nitrogen, but the corrosion problem persists. 15 years of life from the last servicing mission is amazing though. More modern gyros use laser beams, or resonating structure sensors that have no moving mechanical parts and effectively and infinite lifespan. I always wondered why they couldn't be modified for a retrofit into Hubble.

top_comments.text:
Nice overview of Hubble.  I do want to add a couple points:

1.  Many repairs, especially in later missions, involved areas and equipment that were *not* intended to be worked on in space, so NASA had to develop special tools and procedures to do those tasks.  While some maintenance was envisioned for the telescope, most of the work actually performed was not planned and many of the instruments would wound up being replaced entirely.

2.  Hubble's lens flaw *could* have been discovered on the ground by US military equipment normally used with spy satellites of the era.  NASA chose not to allow an examination, apparently because it would cost a few million dollars and put the expensive mirror at risk of damage.

Hubble was designed to higher tolerances than the similar KH spy satellites and thus NASA doubted that the military's equipment could detect any conceivable error.  This assumption turned out to be wrong as though the error seems small in relation to human hairs, it was actually large in relation to specifications; the contractor had failed miserably by assembling their machine incorrectly.  The actual error was truly inconceivable.  If examined by a qualified third party, H

top_comments.author: @thomasackerman5399
top_comments.text:
The Blue Origin subreddit has a lot of actual employees who comment on things, and it's been confirmed that the booster here is real flight hardware with the non-flight interstage forward module section. The booster will serve a similar pathfinder role that the Vulcan Centaur PTT did back in 2021. 

Also missed here in this video is that the Lex Friedman photo shows another forward module, but unlike the non-flight version, there's clearly insulation on it, and it actually has fins installed on it. There is also another midbody seen in the photo, but at the time it was taken over a month ago, it was yet to have any insulation panels, propulsion lines, or electrical lines installed. And this fits in well with what the Wall Street Journal article stated about four boosters in the work.

top_comments.author: @RobbiRobbRobb
top_comments.text: The thing that worries me the most is the almost unavoidable comparison to SpaceX. It took them more than two years from the first fully completed booster to the first flight. And while it is hard to find good data on other rockets, it's probably not too far off with ground testing of both booster and ground systems. We also have yet to see a fully assembled second stage of New Glenn. So while they are obviously making good progress, I don't think the first flight is as close as one might hope.

top_comments.author: @wafikiri_
top_comments.text: Peregrine's valve failure is but one more. Valve failures are too frequent in the space industry to go unnoticed, and they usually cause heavy economic losses, from wet dress rehearsal failures that force withdrawal, fixing, and test repetitions to complete mission failures once in flight. It should demand from engineers the replacement of single valves by fail-safe valve devices already in the design phase of development. A fail-safe device multiplies by four the number of valves needed but requires two unfortunate valve failures, not one, to fail its proper working (two sets of valves in series, each with two valves in parallel, make a single valve failure in the open or closed position irrelevant). The relative cost of using fail-safe valve devices instead of single valves is too low compared to the expectancy of mission failure costs due to valve malfunction.

top_comments.author: @MrGeneralScar
top_comments.text:
32:00 One thing that does stick in my mind regarding tower catch attempts is that unlike Falcon 9 and the Merlin which must do a sucicide burn to land and shut down precisely on queue. Starship with its raptors can deep throttle enough to hover the booster. So this isnt so much of a landing as a come in and hover, then have the tower arms attach to the booster. It is for sure super duper complex manoeuver to pull off and I dont think they will get it on the first try. But wouldnt it be cool if they come in for the hover and see something isnt right and the booster powers up again ascends a bit and hops over to the gulf and splashes down instead to save stage 0 from damage?

Of course we will all know if that is a possibility well before the mission because the license paperwork will identify that extra hop as a possible thing. top_comments.text:
At 6:45 the "pair of disks" is something called a spectacle blind. It's a combination of a blind flange that is used to isolate equipment or piping along with a spacer ring that takes up the gap in the flange while allowing normal flow through the pipe. These are permanently installed in areas that have been identified as a common spot to isolate via blinding when maintenance work needs to be done, and allow for very quick visual inspection as to the blind's orientation (blind or open).

The operations side of running a tank farm full of cryo liquids is largely ignored because people mostly care about "rocket go burrrr" 😂

Without the ops people and the millwrights/pipe fitters, nothing gets off the ground and no welding or pipe work is permitted to happen.

The Turbopumps power the fluid pumps directly. The fluid pumps push the methalox into the preburner which spins the turbopumps. 
So essentially the turbopumps cannot spin without the methalox preburner. This is why starting an engine is the hardest part of an engine. I believe SpaceX uses high pressure liguid nitrogen to start their engines. Cheaper than helium and helium is only required for Hydrogen engines since liquid hydrogen will freeze any nitrogen in the turbopumps or tubing.
They could potentially use electric motors to spin the turbopumps enough for the methalox to run through the system. 
It's a great question but I would imagine they don't keep the turbopumps spinning without the cooling

I wonder if I should tell this story - but oh well....
   My father was George Arthur Jacobs, an aerospace engineer originally from Pennsylvania. He had a last contract in Sunnyvale that was something to do with the space shuttle engines. On the scheduled day of the first launch (which WAS successful) he sat in front of the TV set (what we had in those days) through every single hold and wait. I remember he sat there overnight, unmoving, following the entire process. I had to go to the kitchen and bring food to the man... Until it finally went into orbit, and then he shot up out of his chair, CLAPPED his hands together and said: "THAT'S IT! WE DID IT!!!" 

     ~ and then he took me out to celebrate 😎

  It was one of the most unforgettable moments in time that I remember about MY PAPA

top_comments.author: @MrCrystalcranium
top_comments.text: STS-1 probably came closer to catastrophe than any flight other than the Challenger and Columbia disasters.  The acoustic overpressure was miscalculated in pre-launch preparations and Columbia's body flap was displaced way past its movement range.  It hung down into the reentry plasma much further than the norm and as a consequence, got much hotter than anticipated.  The overpressure shock also broke a support strut on a nitrogen tetroxide tank in Columbia's nose section just behind the control panel.  If the tank had ruptured, the cockpit would have been filled with toxic gas that probably would have destroyed rubber seals around windows and in Young and Crippen's suits killing them.  No more Space Shuttle program if the first flight crew had died.

top_comments.author: @clopterbug1
top_comments.text: My dad helped design n build the shuttle tires for BF Goodrich. My dad got a call from NASA telling him his tire failed upon landing and basically told him he was in a lot of trouble. They shipped the remains of the tire as well as it's mate for testing. After testing, there was nothing wrong with the tire and it wasn't the reason for the failure. The mate tire had some odd wear as if it had been dragged. After some more digging, they found out that the new pilot freaked out and locked the brakes resulting in the blowout. After the Challenger disaster that took the life of my dad's highschool classmate, NASA immediately called my dad saying his tires were the reason for the explosion. He had to prove his tires didn't do it to clear his name. He provided the original tire testing info as well as he had to repeat the tests on tires made the same time the Challenger tires were made. There was no difference in the tires meaning they were identical in results. Also talked to a lady that helped build the breaks and her department was also led to believe that their breaks caused it and had to prove it didn't.

top_comments.author: @b.b.stanfield9829
top_comments.text: Primary reason for the curves on the OLM pieces inside is exactly what Das said. It’s to ensure no single point of failure develops. A square corner will tend to be a stress point and start a crack that then runs through the entire section. Rounding eases and spreads the strain therefore no cracking. In some cases, such as aircraft aluminum, if you get a stress crack at a point which will relieve some of the stress, but you don’t want it to go all the way to failure, you put a small hole at the end of the existing crack. It’s called “stop drilling”. The hole being round has a lot of effect relieving any remaining stress.

Frankly I don't see flight 5 happening in Oktober unless one of these three things are true:
1: The FAA has been sufficiently pressured (and, let's not mince words, "bullied") by the likes of NASA and Congress into moving quickly but quietly to get this over with.
2: The relation between SpaceX and the FAA hasn't become quite as hostile as it seems from the outside, and an acceptable compromise has been worked out.
3: SpaceX has gotten a promise from either NASA/the pentagon or transportation minister Buttigieg that they'll get a waiver exempting this flight from FAA oversight under some "National Security Interest" bollocks premise (something which people on that greatest font of wisdom, reddit, have been repeatedly saying is something that those agencies have the legal power to do, as in "you're being dumb FAA, this is important and safe, go pound sand") and are gambling that even if the FAA flip out, their hands will be tied by those above them, since the FAA is not in fact sovereign and can be dictated to by the likes of Congress and the Pentagon.

Obviously I hope it's option 2, but if a flight does happen this month, it will be interesting to see which one it was.

They have intentionally been going slow because they don't want to build something and then find out after a flight that that needs to radically change. This isn't exactly a secret. If they wanted to, I guarantee you that they could go from starting to stack a ship or a booster through finishing it up to cryo to static fire in like 3 months. Again, if they really needed to. Extrapolating what they're going to build over the next two years based on what they've built over the past two years while this was all still in prototyping and early development phase is not how SpaceX works and you know it.

To spell the upcoming 6-12 months out:
Until tower 2 is ready they're not gonna build more than one booster block 2.
If booster 12 lands (which if that sub-1 cm comment is true I think it will) they will tear it down and incorporate that data to start building the first block 2 booster.
In the meantime they will have boosters 13

top_comments.text: One key difference to remember between Falcon 9 and Superheavy (aside from the droneships being on a heaving sea) is that the Falcon suicide burns into the landing with very little room for error. There is a point in its deceleration profile where the booster absolutely needs to be in contact with the deck and the engines off. The Superheavy (theoretically) can slow down, hover and adjust its position, much like New Sheppard and (theoretically) New Glenn, so, in theory, the margin for error can be larger, at least as much as the landing propellant reserves allow.

The heat shields on IFT 4, 5, and 6 performed as designed during those EDLs that had the same level of heating as a Ship would experience on return from LEO. top_comments.text:
Been a late night, but me being a nerd had to stay up and review the Starliner docking stream to try and find answers. A few pages of notes later and I basically have a transcript.

What I found is Starliner’s flight plan included a manual demo in a hold at 260m. The first thruster failed at the terminal phase initiation burn, and the second failed later after the inbound flyaround burn. After those 2 thrusters failed off, they planned to hot fire the thrusters when they reached that planned hold. Once they reached the manual hold they lost 2 more thrusters. At this point the coms sounded more urgent and they started the hot fire tests.  They looked at the data and began enabling thrusters, then the 5th thruster failed off. They had reenabled enough thrusters at this point to proceed with docking, but they did another round of hot fire tests to bring all but 1 back online.

Edit: A couple more things to add. 1. This demonstration showed me they sort of lost control in 3 degrees, I previously thought it was just forward thrusting, but Das showed that when he pitched and yawed that created unintended backward motion.

top_comments.text: While that 2.2𝝁m error near the edge of Hubble might seem small, optically in this case, it's huge, especially for a mirror 2.4m in diameter.  The Vera Rubin Telescope's primary mirror was designed to have an average error (difference between it's theoretical shape and it's actual shape when finished) of  58.5 nm (36 times smaller than the Hubble defect) and a Peak-to-Valley (the difference between the largest positive and the largest negative surface defect of 161nm, about 14 times smaller than the error in Hubble's surface.  Of course, these two mirrors were designed for different purposes, but they operate in similar wavelengths of light, and the comparison is useful to show how big the error Hubble's primary surface was.

top_comments.text: A risk that Frank Rubio as well as Butch and Suni faced for several weeks was the possibility of returning to Earth without wearing pressure suits, something which mission rules normally don’t allow after the Challenger accident in 1986. Between January 2023 shortly after the Soyuz MS-22 capsule leaked until the uncrewed Soyuz MS-23 replacement capsule arrived in February 2023, Rubio was assigned to the Dragon Crew 5 capsule, where his Sokol space suit would not have functioned.  Similarly from September 6, 2024 when the Boeing Starliner undocked until September 29, 2024 when the Dragon Crew 9 capsule arrived, Butch and Suni were assigned to the Crew 8 capsule. Although a spare SpaceX suit that fit Suni was available, there apparently would have been no way for her to hook up her umbilicals, so like Butch she would have reentered without a pressure suit in an emergency.

top_comments.author: @firefly4f4
top_comments.text:
Atlantis:
At the Cape.  Makes complete sense.

Discovery:
Smithsonian alongside numerous other historical spacecraft.  Also makes sense. Moving it would require either recommissioning a shuttle carrier or shutting down & certifying roadways across multiple states.  Logistical nightmare.

Endeavor:
Doesn't make much sense in California, but will be a full stack display with construction well underway.  Also not going to transport it by road or rail through the Rockies, so would need a carrier; even more of a logistical nightmare.

So why not Enterprise?  It wasn't in space, but was in Houston for publicity and testing, and is on the Intrepid in NYC which makes no sense to me, and should be (relative to the others) easy to barge to the Texas coast and a much shorter road closure/certification.

If a shuttle must be moved (I'd rather not for fear of damaging/losing any in transport) then Enterprise seems to make the most sense by far.

top_comments.author: @officialwaspman
top_comments.text:
My thoughts on the new tank:

I believe that this could be one of 2 things:
   1. This is a tank to test propellant transfer systems with this small tank acting as either the receiving ship, or acting as the tanker ship. They could use this for testing fuel lines and pump systems on the ground and making sure lines up the way it is designed, without having to transfer large amounts of fuel for each test, speeding up the testing time. 

   2. The tank is an internal propellant storage tank for the ship that acts as a tanker. This looks like it could fit in the cargo compartment of a block 3 starship, and could leave space around it for other systems like pumps or other storage. Maybe the article is upside down and the valve on the top is meant to be rotated to a down position towards the top main fuel tank, and then be diverted to fuel lines in the fuel transfer connectors. Or, it is in its flight orientation and the lines transfer down the walls to the 2 connectors in the top half of the ship.

Let me know what y'all think! Did I miss something or get something wrong? I'd love to guess and learn more about this system!!

top_comments.author: @hannesgroesslinger
top_comments.text:
If you hold out your arm, and a bird comes down to sit on your hand, did you catch the bird or did it land on your hand?
In my opinion, it landed.

Wheter you have held out your arm for a long time, or only moved it into place in the very last moment, does not make a difference.
The difference is wheter the bird slowed down on it's own. If the bird planned to fly by, and you grab it out of the air, then it is a catch.

If the action of grabing a flying object is what causes the object to slow down, then it is a catch.
If a flying object slows down on it's own and comes to a rest on a stationary object, then it is a landing.

The chopsticks don't cause the booster to slow down. They move into place almost in the last second, but they then stop moving without causing any deceleration to the booster. The booster decelerates by itself, and then lands on the now stationary chopsticks.

The chopsticks don't catch the booster, they just move the landing spot into place.

A bit of clarification to what Julia said at 2:21:00. If you go to the Kennedy visitor center prior to the SLS launch the paid admission includes a bus ride out to both the recently reopened LC-39 gantry viewing stand and the Saturn V center.  The gantry viewing is actually closer to pad 39B where SLS is than the Saturn V center. The gantry is  just 2.2 miles away from 39B, and has more of a straight on view, whereas the Saturn V center is 3.3 miles away from 39B and has a view slightly to the side. Both are great views, and again both are included in the "free" bus tour that is included with visitor center admission.  You can stay at each viewing location as long as you want before getting on the next available bus to go to the next stop, but be aware that the buses stop going to the gantry viewing after 2:00 pm, at least when I was there. Also the lines for the bus tour get longer as the day goes on so it's usually best to go on the bus tour when you first get there.

There are also special bus tours called the Explore Tour which you can purchase for an additional $30. This takes you to a viewing location between pads 39A and 39B known as the A/B camera stop where you can view

top_comments.text:
Kinda sad that the easiest replacement for SLS and Orion was not discussed during that part. If you're binning SLS, you really shouldn't try to slap Orion on top of another non-human rated rocket. Just cancel Orion too at that point. You can go to the moon and back without it. The HLS landers that are going to fly on Artemis IV and V need to be refueled in LEO and are designed to do LEO->NRHO->lunar surface-> NRHO. Which takes roughly 8.1 km/s of delta-V, you can lower it to 7.4 if you switch NRHO with low lunar orbit, which is why SpaceX and Blue Origin requested that. Anyway, to do LEO->low lunar orbit->LEO takes, even with zero aerobraking on the way back, 7.9 km/s. There's your alternative. Take a dragon up to LEO and just use a second HLS lander to go from LEO to lunar orbit and back. Done, and done. Artemis IV and V will have already demonstrated the required capability (in-space refueling and keeping their crews alive near and on the moon) to remove SLS and Orion completely.

Big waste of fuel of course to not use the atmosphere to slow down when coming back, but this architecture only needs to be done for a few years until either Starship or Blue Origin's hopefully-coming-s

top_comments.author: @cinemaformer1474
top_comments.text:
I was born in 1961, so I grew up with the Apollo program. I can still remember the day of the first moon landing vividly; the whole family was gathered in front of the TV, which back then was still black-and-white and had only two channels. The sound was poor, and the picture quality, by today’s standards, was pretty pixelated. 
Still, by the standards of the time, it was the event of a lifetime. Over the years, I’ve learned a lot about the missions and watched them, and even today, that mission remains the benchmark for me. What was achieved back then with the resources available still borders on magic to me. The sense of unity in achieving a goal and never losing sight of the focus is what shaped me. Nothing was left out, no one was abandoned, and there was no distinction between black and white. 
Today, visual communication takes 1.37 seconds to travel a distance of over 400,000 km, and the quality is as if the crew were just down the hall making a phone call. Unbelievable—Thank You to everyone for this effort, and I wish the crew a safe journey.

IFT 12 went *_much_* better than I expected! With so many changes, I was determined to be satisfied as long as it didn't destroy Stage Zero. To get past stage separation would make the mission a big success, because it would mean that useful test data was obtained for both booster and ship. For ship to successfully reenter, on target, in the Indian Ocean, was beyond what I dared hope.

top_comments.author: @Yrouel86
top_comments.text:
Calling the Commercial Crew Program a failure is ridiculous.

Not only it was successful because having dissimilar redundancy worked as intended but it also proved that the commercial way, in other words not cost plus, works and enables NASA to get immense capabilities at a bargain.

If NASA had to develop that capability the usual old way it would've cost at least 10x more than what costed SpaceX (I'm based this estimate on what would've cost NASA to develop just a Falcon 9 equivalent from a study they did back then where they determined that for NASA it would've been $4 billion the usual way or $2 billion at least trying to be efficient...SpaceX did it with $400 million).

By EJ logic it would be perfectly fine for NASA to waste that money to do it themselves instead of being a SpaceX customer....

videos.title: China Lands Orbital-Class Booster for First Time - Historic Success | This Week in Spaceflight

top_comments.author: @iCuteJP
top_comments.text: Aircraft carrier arresting cables have a breaking strength of roughly 150 to 250 tonnes-force and routinely stop 20 to 30-tonne aircraft landing at around 240 to 280 km/h. A reusable rocket capture is a different problem. The booster is not in free fall during the final capture. Its engines reduce the descent speed to near zero, so the cables only need to absorb the remaining kinetic energy and stabilize the vehicle. The reported Chinese system also uses about 8 cables with electromagnetic damping, allowing the load to be distributed and reducing peak forces. With high-strength cables and multiple load paths, the system should have a significant safety margin if the design specifications are correct. Whether it proves reliable in repeated real-world operations remains to be seen, but the underlying engineering principles and physics are sound.

top_comments.text:
Watched your coverage of today's Booster 21 static fire. Good angles, good info — and I say that as someone who watches a lot of your streams.

One thing didn't need to be there. In chat, teyton90 asked why the OLM isn't higher up with a deeper flame trench. Ryan Weber's answer amounted to "the way it is right now, it works perfectly fine" — delivered as if the question were dumb for having been asked.

It isn't a naive question. It's the question SpaceX asked itself and answered. Pad 1's mount was destroyed on Booster 7's launch in April 2023, and every Starship pad built since — Pad B at Starbase, LC-39A, SLC-37 — has a flame trench. NSF's own reporting has followed that trench work piling by piling. So when a viewer asks why the mount isn't higher and the trench deeper, he's asking about the single biggest design change in the pad program, and the answer he got was that the current arrangement is fine as is.

So a viewer asking about trench depth and mount height is asking a question you could have spent two good minutes on. Instead he got told he was wrong for wondering. That's a bad trade for a channel whose whole value is explaining hardware to people who want to unders

top_comments.text: Asking me what I think about Starbase Louisiana makes me think about the first time I saw the plans for Starship. The Falcon 9 booster was still years away from a successful landing. I thought, "That monster will never be built, let alone get off the launch pad. They can't even get Falcon 9's booster to land." Falcon's booster did land, hundreds of time. The Falcon 9 is currently the most successful launch vehicle in the world and Starship has since got off the launch pad 13 times. So, now I think that the things SpaceX really wants to do will most likely (eventually) get done, including Starbase Louisiana.

top_comments.text:
@NSF My 2 cents on operational vs test flight…
Starship (ship and booster) are conceptually designed and intended to be reusable. Therefore, until they can launch / catch / reuse the vehicles reliably, they cannot be considered  operational. Yes they may be able to deliver operational payloads, but as a system, starship is still in testing phase. No v3 booster has been reliably caught and reused. Obviously, no starship has been caught and re-used either.
